title: Ci e Ne
subtitle: Two small particles that replace a place, a topic, or a quantity.
objectives: Use ci to replace a place or a topic introduced by a, in, su
Use ne to replace a quantity or a topic introduced by di
Place ci and ne correctly relative to the verb

content.intro: You already met ci inside c'è/ci sono — now meet its full range, alongside its partner particle ne, both of which let you avoid repeating a place, topic, or quantity you've already mentioned.
content.explanation: Ci replaces a place ("there") or a phrase introduced by a/in/su: Vai a Roma? Sì, ci vado domani. (Are you going to Rome? Yes, I'm going [there] tomorrow.) Ne replaces a quantity, or a phrase introduced by di: Quanti libri hai? Ne ho tre. (How many books do you have? I have three [of them].)

rules.heading: a) Ci — place and topic (a/in/su)
rules.body:
• Place: Sei mai stato in Sicilia? Sì, ci sono stato l'anno scorso.
  • Topic (pensare a): Pensi al tuo futuro? Sì, ci penso spesso.

rules.heading: b) Ne — quantity and topic (di)
rules.body:
• Quantity: Vuoi del vino? Sì, ne vorrei un po'.
  • Topic (parlare di): Parli di politica? Non ne parlo mai.

rules.heading: c) Position
rules.body: Both go before a conjugated verb, or attach to an infinitive: Ci vado. / Voglio andarci. With a number/quantity + passato prossimo, the participle agrees with ne's quantity: Quante mele hai comprato? Ne ho comprate cinque.

examples.it: Vai spesso in palestra? Sì, ci vado tre volte a settimana.
examples.en: Do you go to the gym often? Yes, I go [there] three times a week.

examples.it: Quanti fratelli hai? Ne ho due.
examples.en: How many siblings do you have? I have two [of them].

examples.it: Credi in questo progetto? Sì, ci credo davvero.
examples.en: Do you believe in this project? Yes, I really believe in it.

examples.it: Vuoi ancora del caffè? No grazie, non ne voglio più.
examples.en: Do you want more coffee? No thanks, I don't want any more [of it].

examples.it: Ne ho parlato con il mio capo.
examples.en: I talked about it with my boss.

commonMistakes.why: Ci goes before the conjugated verb, exactly like other object pronouns — not after it.
A bare number needs ne to stand in for "of them" — Italian can't drop the quantity's referent the way casual English sometimes does.

commonMistakes.wrong: Ne ho comprato cinque mele. (both ne and the noun)
commonMistakes.right: Ho comprato cinque mele. / Ne ho comprate cinque.
commonMistakes.why: Ne replaces the noun — using both ne and the noun together in the same clause is redundant.

items.prompt: Vai in Italia quest'estate? Sì, ___ vado ad agosto.
Pensi spesso al futuro? Sì, ___ penso ogni giorno.
"Do you want some water?" — "Yes, I want a little [of it]."

summary: Ci replaces a place or a topic introduced by a/in/su.
Ne replaces a quantity or a topic introduced by di.
Both go before the conjugated verb; ne with a number forces participle agreement in the passato prossimo.
